summary: A case study of a several-hour ARPANET disruption in October 1980, when a high-priority software process ran out of control. It explains the symptoms and causes, and what lessons network designers can draw.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 789 explains an ARPANET outage caused by a hardware fault that corrupted routing information. The damaged updates circulated repeatedly, consuming resources until operators told the network to ignore updates from the faulty machine.

subtitle: How corrupted routing updates helped trigger an ARPANET-wide outage.

tldr.problem: A hardware fault caused corrupted routing updates to circulate and consume resources on ARPANET Interface Message Processors.
tldr.mechanism: The memo traces how damaged sequence numbers made three versions of one update appear newer than one another, keeping them circulating.
tldr.outcome: The outage was cleared by ignoring updates from the malfunctioning IMP; the case highlights limits in protocol and hardware safeguards.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 789's status as Unknown. The RFC is a case study of a particular ARPANET outage and the failure mechanisms that contributed to it.

sections.title: The Network Stops Carrying Traffic
sections.content:
On October 27, 1980, most ARPANET IMPs could not communicate reliably with one another for several hours. Existing connections broke, and attempts to reach hosts on other IMPs reported that no physical path existed.

Restarting individual IMPs did not solve the problem because they received the same routing updates again after reconnecting. The investigation found many queued updates from a single malfunctioning IMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the network could not pass traffic between IMPs. Restarting one machine did not help because the bad routing updates reached it again.

sections.title: How Routing Updates Were Circulated
sections.content:
Each IMP periodically sent neighbors a routing update listing its immediate neighbors and average packet delay. The update used a 6-bit sequence number, and IMPs forwarded updates they considered newer so the information spread through the network.

Sequence numbers wrapped around. The comparison rule was designed to tell which update was later, but it assumed that updates from the same IMP would not form a cycle of mutually newer values.
sections.plainLanguage: IMPs shared information about their routes and used sequence numbers to recognize newer updates. The sequence number had a limited range and eventually wrapped around.

sections.title: Corruption Creates a Routing Update Loop
sections.content:
Queued updates from IMP 50 repeatedly had sequence numbers 8, 40, and 44. Under the comparison rule, each number could be judged later than another, creating a cycle that kept the updates circulating and used CPU time and buffer space.

The authors infer that a hardware fault at a neighboring IMP dropped bits while an update was being recreated for retransmission. Packet checksums detected damaged packets, but the stored routing tables used to recreate them were not checked every time they were accessed.
sections.plainLanguage: Bit damage changed an update's sequence number. The routing rule then treated the competing versions as newer in a cycle, so the network kept processing them.

sections.title: Recovery and Lessons from the Outage
sections.content:
Operators restored service by patching IMPs to disregard updates from IMP 50, which was already down. The author says that restarting all IMPs at the same time would have cleared the inconsistent routing tables more quickly, but controlling machines through a network-wide outage was difficult.

The memo argues that careful resource limits and protocol design need a way to detect runaway high-priority processes and recover from faults that evade safeguards. It also notes that the proposed sequence-number change would prevent this specific cycle but could not rule out every related failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Ignoring the faulty IMP's updates restored the network. The author recommends detecting resource-consuming failures and making recovery easier, alongside careful protocol design.
